A builder converted four RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell cards (96 GB GDDR7, 600 W) to waterblocks. One card failed: a VRM choke was found loose on the workbench. After the fix they got back to 41k tok/s. That card had passed bring-up and ran fine at light loads for a week before failing.

Author's lesson from the failing card: driver swaps, CUDA reinstalls and inference-engine theories were dead ends that cost hours, and the failure pattern itself should have pointed to the hardware earlier.

Commenter on the failed card's photos: the solder on the choke (inductor) looks terrible and something went wrong in manufacturing. The solder should have wicked across the entire pad, not just a small square, and there should be no brown discoloration.

IPC-610 certified tech: the VRM solder is still in its stencil-applied state and never flowed across the contacts on either the component or the board. They call it a manufacturer reflow-oven defect, a poorly done joint rather than a cracked one.

The author advised not to RMA the card and to have a local phone-repair microsolder tech reattach the part cheaply. A commenter pushed back: a card with this defect could be an all-round lemon that should not have passed QA, and a week of working fine doesn't prove it good, so RMA is the safer call.

Critic: the RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell is SM120, so it has no tmem/tcgen05 and lacks support in the main libraries, which focus on B300/SM100. For the price of 4 cards they'd buy a single B300: similar total AI TOPS and bandwidth, about 25% less memory, half the energy, and better SM interconnect. Or just rent.
Power concern for a 4-card build: about 2.4 kW is well beyond a standard US circuit. The commenter asks whether people install 240V/30A circuits or repurpose dryer, EV-charger or hot-tub circuits.

Reacting to the MSRP reportedly doubling to $16,000: a Mac Studio with 96GB of unified memory costs $5,299, matching the card's 96GB of GDDR7. The commenter questions why CUDA still commands an ~$11k price premium.
Alternative suggested instead of the $16k card: six AMD R9700s with an older 5965WX Threadripper and 128GB DDR4 to run DeepSeek V4 Flash lossless, and pocket the remaining $6,000.
